h1: RJ Mitte, Breaking Bad's Walt Jr.: A Tribute Documentary
seo_title: RJ Mitte Tribute: Breaking Bad's Walt Jr. | Documentary
meta_description: A tribute to RJ Mitte, who played Walt Jr. on Breaking Bad: his childhood with cerebral palsy, how he got the role, his disability advocacy and his later work.
dek: A tribute to RJ Mitte, the actor with cerebral palsy who played Walter White Jr. on Breaking Bad and spent his career pushing for disabled performers to be seen.

sections.heading: Growing up with cerebral palsy
paragraphs: Roy Frank Mitte III was born on 21 August 1992 in Jackson, Mississippi, and adopted a few weeks later. At three he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, a condition that affects movement and muscle control. His childhood brought months with his legs in casts, then leg braces, crutches and years of physical, occupational and speech therapy; he said he stopped wearing the braces at 13. Around then his family moved to Los Angeles, where he found work as an extra, including on Hannah Montana. He later said he started acting to meet kids his own age.

sections.heading: Becoming Flynn
paragraphs: Breaking Bad's creator, Vince Gilligan, based Walter White's son on a friend with cerebral palsy. Walt Jr.'s condition was more severe than Mitte's own, so he learned to walk on crutches and to slow and blur his speech, in effect unlearning some of his therapy. The show premiered in January 2008, when he was 15, and over five seasons he appeared in nearly every episode. The cast won the Screen Actors Guild award for drama ensemble, and Variety's Daniel D'Addario called his performance a breakthrough for disability representation.

sections.heading: Years of advocacy
bullets: Bullied as a child, he started an anti-bullying campaign on YouTube in 2010 and took the message into schools and onto college campuses for years.
He was a youth ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy, a Screen Actors Guild spokesman for performers with disabilities, an ambassador for Shriners Children's and president of The Mitte Foundation.
SAG-AFTRA gave him its Harold Russell Award in 2013.
His advice to others was not to hide a disability. In 2014 he told the Associated Press his own was "an asset instead of something that would hinder."

sections.heading: Work after Breaking Bad
paragraphs: In 2014 he joined Switched at Birth as Campbell, a pre-med student who uses a wheelchair after a snowboarding accident. He appeared in a Gap campaign and walked for Vivienne Westwood, and in 2016 he was part of Channel 4's presenting team for the Rio Paralympic Games. He played a young man with muscular dystrophy in Who's Driving Doug, and in Triumph (2021), which he also executive produced, a high-school student with cerebral palsy fighting to become a wrestler; NBC News reported the film earned a Ruderman Family Foundation seal for authentic representation. His film Talking to Strangers premiered on 30 September 2026. In October 2025 he became engaged to Kennedy Suarez, his partner since 2018 after a long friendship.

sections.heading: How he is remembered
paragraphs: Mitte died on 12 October 2026 in Brownsville, Texas, the city he had moved to. He was 34. His representatives said he died by suicide; when the film was published on 13 October 2026, officials had not released an official cause or manner of death, and an autopsy had been ordered. His representatives asked for privacy for his family. Tributes came from Bryan Cranston, who played his father, as well as Aaron Paul, Dean Norris, Marlee Matlin, Lea Thompson, AMC, United Cerebral Palsy and SAG-AFTRA. A public celebration of his life was planned for 16 October 2026 at The Mitte Arts and Cultural Center in Brownsville, and his family asked for donations to cerebral palsy research in lieu of flowers. The film follows media guidelines on reporting suicide and does not discuss how he died or speculate about why.
